purpose: Literature-grounded introductory revision for the power-system agent tutorial. Definitions and teaching examples only; no new performance measurements.

editorial_position.consensus: Do not claim a universal definition. State which classical or LLM-engineering usage is being used.
editorial_position.working_definition: Here, agentic AI means a system in which an AI model helps choose and revise actions toward a goal using feedback, within an explicitly bounded operating process.
editorial_position.status: Original tutorial working definition synthesized from DEF01-DEF03, not a quotation or standardized taxonomy.
editorial_position.scope: The opening must distinguish a classical agent abstraction from the narrower LLM-agent pattern studied in this tutorial. Agentic does not require multiple agents, an LLM is not required by classical agency, and the word does not establish correctness or operating authority.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, Chapter 2: Intelligent Agents
sources.bibliographic_citation: Russell, Stuart J., and Peter Norvig. Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach. 2nd ed. Upper Saddle River, NJ: Prentice Hall, 2003. Chapter 2, Intelligent Agents, pp. 32-58. Author-hosted chapter draft dated 2002.
sources.type: Canonical authored textbook; primary exposition of its agent framework
sources.version_note: Despite its current /4th-ed/ URL, the verified sample chapter is the older chapter with printed pages 32-58 and 2002 directory timestamp. Do not cite this PDF as fourth-edition text. The official second-edition page identifies the edition and Prentice Hall; the final book citation is 2003.
sources.paraphrased_definition: An agent is viewed through its interaction with an environment: it receives percepts and produces actions. An agent function describes the mapping from percept history to action, while a program implements it. The text treats agency as an analytical viewpoint rather than an absolute classification.
sources.teaching_use: Establish the broad historical concept before introducing LLM control loops. Software files, messages and tool results can form the environment; a physical robot is unnecessary.
sources.caveat: Rationality is defined relative to evidence and a performance measure; it is not guaranteed success. This broad definition alone does not distinguish a modern LLM agent from ordinary software.

sources.title: Intelligent agents: theory and practice
sources.bibliographic_citation: Wooldridge, Michael, and Nicholas R. Jennings. Intelligent agents: theory and practice. The Knowledge Engineering Review 10, no. 2 (June 1995): 115-152. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0269888900008122.
sources.type: Primary theoretical/architectural research review by the authors
sources.version_note: The author-hosted HTML is an earlier draft stamped November 1994. Use the final 1995 PDF for the bibliographic citation; the HTML makes the definition sections searchable. The final PDF is image-based in the web extractor, so section locators are safer than an unverified PDF page number.
locators: Section 1.1.1, A Weak Notion of Agency
sources.paraphrased_definition: Their weak notion groups autonomy, interaction with others, timely response to environmental changes, and goal-directed initiative. A stronger usage additionally invokes mental-state concepts. They explicitly discuss the absence of one universally accepted definition.
sources.teaching_use: Use the four properties as questions about behavior, not a modern vendor certification checklist.
sources.caveat: These are the authors' historical conceptual distinctions. Neither multiple LLM roles nor a tool-calling interface alone demonstrates all four properties.

sources.title: Building effective agents
sources.bibliographic_citation: Erik S. and Barry Zhang. Building effective agents. Anthropic Engineering, December 19, 2024. Live article reviewed October 17, 2026.
sources.type: Official practitioner architecture account by the system maintainers
sources.paraphrased_definition: Their engineering terminology places both workflows and agents under agentic systems. Workflow control follows predefined code paths; an agent lets the LLM direct its process and tool use. They acknowledge multiple meanings of agent.
sources.caveat: Present this as an attributed architectural convention. Their workflows can include model-based routing, dynamic worker decomposition and refinement loops, so conditional edges or a loop are not sufficient tests for agency.
sources.version_note: The live page now warns that tooling has changed since the original publication. Use its conceptual distinction, not its present SDK list as a claim about the 2024 implementation.

sources.title: LangGraph overview; Tools
sources.author: LangChain maintainers
sources.bibliographic_citation: LangChain maintainers. LangGraph overview and Tools. Docs by LangChain, Python open-source documentation. Accessed October 17, 2026.
sources.type: Official framework and tool-interface documentation; two pages in one documentation collection
locators: LangGraph overview: opening paragraphs and product-role list
Tools: opening definition and Basic tool definition
sources.paraphrased_definition: LangGraph is an orchestration framework/runtime for stateful execution, combining programmed and model-driven steps. A tool exposes a callable function through defined inputs and outputs; its description and schema guide invocation.
sources.teaching_use: Separate orchestration from decision policy and numerical computation. The same runtime can execute a fixed process or an LLM-directed loop.
sources.caveat: A framework's capabilities do not prove that a particular application uses them. A tool is an interface role and may wrap a complex service or another agent. Do not universally equate tool with a trivial or stateless function.

sources.title: PowerAgent: Open-Source Agentic AI for Power Grids
sources.author: Power and AI Initiative, Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences
sources.bibliographic_citation: Power and AI Initiative, Harvard SEAS. PowerAgent: Open-Source Agentic AI for Power Grids. Official project website. Accessed October 17, 2026.
sources.type: Official domain-platform description by its maintainers
locators: PowerFM / PowerMCP / PowerWF / PowerSkills component descriptions
sources.paraphrased_definition: The official site describes PowerAgent as an open-source community/platform developing power-domain models, software interfaces, workflows and skills.
sources.caveat: PowerAgent is a proper name for a domain ecosystem, not the generic definition of agent and not one fixed agent architecture. Describe the specific PowerAgent application, simulator and task when making capability claims.

distinctions.question: What perceives and acts in this environment?
distinctions.tutorial_meaning: A broad interaction model; implementations may use rules, planning, optimization, learning or LLMs.

distinctions.question: Does the model help decide the next action from observed results?
distinctions.tutorial_meaning: A goal-directed decision component in an execution loop. Prompts, state, runtime and tool interfaces support the model; model weights alone are not the whole application.

distinctions.question: What operation can be invoked with specified arguments?
distinctions.tutorial_meaning: Callable capability, such as a power-flow run, record read or evidence check. The caller/orchestrator determines when it runs.

distinctions.question: How are steps and their dependencies arranged?
distinctions.tutorial_meaning: An executable process may prescribe steps, branches and checks. It may contain LLM calls or agent components. A DAG expresses dependencies; cycles support repeated steps.

distinctions.question: How does the assembled system pursue the task?
distinctions.tutorial_meaning: A system/approach label rather than an extra component beside an agent. State the adopted usage; a single agent can participate in such a system.

distinctions.question: What executes and persists the orchestration?
distinctions.tutorial_meaning: A general software framework/runtime, usable for both fixed and model-directed processes.

distinctions.question: Which domain ecosystem or application is being discussed?
distinctions.tutorial_meaning: A named power-system community/platform. Name a concrete application for architecture or result claims.

power_example.status: Original hypothetical teaching example; not a measured paper trace or claim of deployed control authority.
power_example.request: Investigate why the base-case AC power flow on frozen network v43 fails, then return an evidence-backed report within two retries.
power_example.environment_and_observations: Frozen network data, solver logs, returned convergence status and validation results.
power_example.tool_contract: Return converged, numerical diagnostics and an artifact identifier; return an explicit error on failure. This interface is illustrative.
power_example.fixed_workflow_variant: A programmed process always loads v43, runs the solver, validates the output and reports status. On failure it follows a predefined diagnostic branch.
power_example.agent_variant: Within allowed read-only diagnostics and a retry budget, an LLM chooses which missing evidence to inspect next from the observed failure; it can stop, request clarification or escalate.
power_example.orchestration_role: LangGraph could carry state, execute chosen nodes, route validation outcomes and checkpoint the process. It does not supply the electrical model or certify the diagnosis.
power_example.domain_platform_role: PowerAgent components can provide domain interfaces or workflows; claim a particular implementation only when its paper/code identifies it.
power_example.success: A complete report distinguishes a solved case from an unresolved failure and cites the exact evidence and network version. No live switching action is included.

slide_outlines.title: What is an agent? Start with an environment and actions
points: Classical AI studies a system through what it observes and what it does.
An LLM is one possible decision mechanism; agency predates LLMs.
slide_outlines.example: A study assistant observes solver logs and acts by requesting another diagnostic run or reporting a result.
slide_outlines.note: Use Russell/Norvig's broad lens first; avoid saying all older automation fails to qualify as an agent.

slide_outlines.title: What is agentic AI in this tutorial?
points: We study AI-supported action selection toward a goal, revised using feedback.
The task also has explicit permissions, budgets and stopping rules.
slide_outlines.note: Label this as the tutorial's working definition. Keep autonomy relative to the assigned task; it does not mean unrestricted action.

slide_outlines.title: A tool performs a call; an agent chooses what to do next
points: run_pf(v43, base) is a callable capability with an input/output contract.
The agent can use its result to choose another permitted diagnostic, stop or escalate.
slide_outlines.note: This is a component-role distinction, not a claim that a tool can never contain another agent. Show the returned error as an observation.

slide_outlines.title: Workflow and agent describe different choices about control
points: A workflow can prescribe the study sequence and validation gates.
An LLM agent can choose some next steps inside that process.
slide_outlines.note: Attribute fixed-code-path versus dynamic-direction terminology to Anthropic. A router, refinement loop or worker allocation can still be an engineered workflow; diagrams alone do not determine agency.

slide_outlines.title: LangGraph and PowerAgent occupy different roles
points: PowerAgent names a power-domain ecosystem; its particular applications combine models, tools and workflows.
slide_outlines.note: Do not call either a numerical grid solver. Do not assume every PowerAgent component uses LangGraph. State the actual paper implementation later.

slide_outlines.title: Describe the engineering contract before judging the agent
points: Name the goal, observed evidence, permitted actions and success test.
Keep model choice, tool behavior and orchestration behavior separately inspectable.
slide_outlines.example: For v43, accept an evidenced diagnosis or an explicit unresolved report; do not silently reuse v42 results.
slide_outlines.note: Original bridge into the existing simulator, checkpoint and validation material. A credible system description is more informative than an agentic label.

diagram_suggestion.title: The decision loop and the machinery around it
diagram_suggestion.purpose: Give one concrete, legible distinction between agent, tool, orchestration and domain environment.
diagram_suggestion.sketch: Left: Goal 'diagnose base case v43'. Center: one 'LLM decision' node. Right: 'run_pf(v43, base)' tool, then a 'frozen case + solver' environment. Orthogonal return arrow labeled 'convergence / error / artifact' feeds the decision node. A thin enclosing bracket labeled 'LangGraph: state and execution' surrounds the decision/tool loop. Below, one terminal 'report or escalate' node. Put PowerAgent in the caption as a domain ecosystem, not as a nested physical layer or a claim of this implementation.
diagram_suggestion.layout: Use the existing 14.2 x 4.2 cm native TikZ style, 12.5 pt main labels, a single horizontal action path with a bottom feedback return, no table or UI-card grid.
diagram_suggestion.caption: Original teaching abstraction. Agent names the decision role; tool names the callable interface; orchestration executes the process. The proposed v43 example is illustrative.
assumptions: A tool's internals may be complex.
No claim that PowerAgent always uses LangGraph.
Read-only study diagnostics, no live switching or new performance result.

avoid_claims: There is one universally accepted definition of agentic AI.
An agent must be an LLM or a multi-agent team.
Any tool call, feedback loop or graph automatically makes an application an LLM agent.
A tool is necessarily simple, stateless, deterministic or incapable of wrapping an agent.
LangGraph supplies domain reasoning or numerical grid correctness.
PowerAgent is one agent architecture, or every PowerAgent application uses LangGraph.
Autonomy means unrestricted physical authority, or self-reflection guarantees learning and correctness.
